analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their spouses from holding or trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a Senate committee the day it was introduced, drew zero cosponsors, and died without a hearing or vote when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar members of Congress and their spouses from holding, buying, or selling individual stocks, stock options, futures, or commodities while the member is in office. Diversified mutual funds, exchange-traded funds, and Treasury bonds would still be allowed, and members could comply by putting holdings in a blind trust or selling within 180 days. Profits from violations would go to the Treasury, with civil fines possible.
analysis.who_benefits: The general public, whose trust in government is damaged when lawmakers can trade stocks in companies their own decisions move. The bill also protects honest members by removing the temptation and the appearance of trading on nonpublic information.

how_it_helps.text: Members of Congress and their spouses would be prohibited from holding, purchasing, or selling individual securities, security futures, commodities, or comparable synthetic investments such as options and warrants during the member's term of service.
Any profit from a violating transaction or holding would be disgorged to the U.S. Treasury, and the member could face a civil fine assessed by the applicable ethics committee.
Each member would have to certify compliance annually, the certifications would be published online, and the Government Accountability Office would audit compliance within two years of enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their spouses, who would have to divest individual stocks, options, futures, and commodities (within 180 days of enactment) or place them in a blind trust, giving up direct investing in individual companies while in office.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their spouses

drawbacks.text: Enforcement would run through the Senate and House ethics committees — bodies made up of members of Congress themselves — and a fined member could appeal the fine to a vote of the full Senate or House, so members would largely police their own peers.
Members could keep substantial investments through qualified blind trusts, so the bill restricts direct trading rather than eliminating members' financial holdings.

The strongest good-faith objection to a blanket ban is that it bars even prudent, unrelated investing: members and spouses could no longer own stock in any individual company, and the bill grants ethics committees discretion to grant compliance extensions for members making good-faith divestment efforts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — removing the appearance and opportunity of lawmakers trading on their own official actions — is significant for public trust, and the bill leaves members normal diversified funds and Treasury bonds. Its main weakness is that enforcement is entrusted to the members' own ethics committees, with appeal to the full chamber, which could make fines rare. The divestment requirement is real but manageable given the 180-day window and blind-trust option.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Josh Hawley introduced the Banning Insider Trading in Congress Act on January 13, 2022.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
No senator cosponsored the bill; the cosponsor count was zero for its entire life.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote; the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

The bill would have prohibited members and spouses from holding or trading individual securities, futures, commodities, and comparable derivatives during a member's term, with exceptions for blind trusts and a 180-day window to sell.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting members of Congress kept their ability to hold and trade individual stocks, options, and commodities while in office, and no new divestment, certification, or audit rules were created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress who kept trading

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Missouri; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee; attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a Senate floor vote on any ban on congressional stock trading during the 117th Congress, including this bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. The bill had one Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern on the merits is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their spouses (incumbent officeholders)
industries.note: The bill would strip sitting lawmakers and their spouses of the ability to hold or trade individual stocks, options, futures, and commodities while in office — a channel where their own legislative and oversight work can move prices. Their interest in keeping that channel runs against the public's interest in lawmaking that is not influenced by personal portfolios.
